beats.caption: Inside an AI rack, thick copper cables tie every server to the switch
beats.text: Each GPU server has several 400G or 800G network ports, and they all run up to a top-of-rack switch a metre or two away. These short hops are the most numerous links in a cluster. For years they were passive copper (DAC) cables, but at 100G+ per lane passive copper stops reaching.

beats.caption: An AEC is copper cable with a small chip in each plug
beats.text: An active electrical cable keeps the cheap twinax copper in the middle and adds a retimer or DSP chip inside each connector shell. The plug looks and fits like any other QSFP or OSFP module, so the switch and NIC need no changes.

beats.caption: The chip in the plug cleans up and resends every lane
beats.text: Signals arriving over the copper are blurred and weak. The chip equalizes them, recovers the clock and retransmits a fresh signal, in both directions, for every lane. It draws a few watts per end, much less than the lasers and DSP in an optical module.

beats.caption: Passive copper reaches 1-2 m at 100G+; an AEC reaches 3-7 m
beats.text: Loss in copper grows with length and frequency, so passive cables shrink with each speed step: about 2 m at 100G per lane and roughly 1 m at 200G. The retimer resets the loss budget, stretching copper to around 7 m, enough to span a rack or reach the neighbour.

beats.caption: Cheaper and lower power than optics for short links
beats.text: Optics would work over any distance but cost more, use more power and fail more often. For in-rack and rack-to-rack links AECs win, and hyperscalers now buy them by the million. Related: Credo (CRDO), Marvell (MRVL), Astera Labs (ALAB), Amphenol (APH).
